nameStory: The Great Shearwater gets its name from its incredible ability to 'shear' through ocean waves, gliding just inches above the water's surface with barely a wingbeat. The word 'shear' comes from the Old English meaning 'to cut,' perfectly describing how these birds slice through the air between wave crests. They're called 'great' because they're among the largest members of the shearwater family.
description: The Great Shearwater is a large seabird about the size of a small gull, with long, narrow wings built for gliding over ocean waves. These sleek birds have a distinctive dark cap on their heads, white underparts, and grayish-brown backs that help them blend with the churning sea. They're master ocean travelers, spending most of their lives flying over open water far from shore. You'll typically see them during boat trips or from coastal headlands, where they appear as graceful, stiff-winged gliders riding the ocean swells.

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies with stiff, straight wings held in a slight downward angle, rarely flapping as it glides effortlessly just above the waves in long, sweeping arcs

idTips.label: Head pattern
idTips.description: Dark brownish cap extends from the bill down past the eye, creating a distinctive 'capped' appearance that contrasts sharply with white cheeks and throat

idTips.label: Wing shape
idTips.description: Long, narrow wings that appear almost tube-like when viewed from below, much longer proportionally than a gull's wings

idTips.label: Body coloring
idTips.description: Clean white belly and underwings with grayish-brown back and wings, creating a two-toned appearance when seen from the side

idTips.label: Bill appearance
idTips.description: Dark, hooked bill that looks thick and sturdy, designed for grabbing fish and squid from the water's surface

idTips.label: Size comparison
idTips.description: Noticeably larger than most gulls you'd see from shore, with a more streamlined, torpedo-like body shape

habitat: Great Shearwaters live in the open Atlantic Ocean, rarely coming close to shore except during storms or when feeding. In New England waters, you'll spot them from whale-watching boats, ferries, or coastal headlands during migration periods. They prefer deep offshore waters where they can find their favorite prey of fish and squid.

seasonality.spring: Begin arriving in New England waters in late spring as they migrate north from their Southern Hemisphere breeding grounds. Look for them from boats heading to offshore fishing areas.
seasonality.summer: Most abundant in New England waters during summer months, when they're feeding in our nutrient-rich offshore areas. This is your best time to see them from whale-watching trips.
seasonality.fall: Still present in good numbers through early fall as they continue feeding before beginning their long journey back south. Often seen in mixed flocks with other seabirds.
seasonality.winter: Rarely seen in New England waters as they've migrated back to southern oceans. Any winter sightings are unusual and worth reporting to local birding groups.

funFact: Great Shearwaters are among the world's greatest long-distance commuters, traveling roughly 40,000 miles each year in a figure-eight pattern across the entire Atlantic Ocean—that's like flying around Earth nearly twice annually!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with gulls when seen at a distance, but remember that shearwaters have much stiffer wings and glide close to the water, while gulls flap more frequently and fly at various heights. Think 'stiff surfer' for shearwaters versus 'flappy scavenger' for gulls.
contextualKnowledge: Unlike most birds you see in New England that nest locally, Great Shearwaters are just visiting—they actually nest on remote islands in the South Atlantic like Tristan da Cunha, making them true global wanderers that treat our waters like a seasonal restaurant.
compareHints: Great Shearwaters are larger and cleaner-looking than their close relative, the Sooty Shearwater, which appears uniformly dark brown all over. While Sooty Shearwaters look like they're wearing a dark wetsuit, Great Shearwaters have the classic seabird pattern of dark above and white below. Great Shearwaters also have that distinctive dark cap, while Sooties have dark heads that blend into their overall dusky coloring.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative the Great Shearwater, the sooty shearwater is smaller, uniformly dark, and lacks the Great Shearwater's distinctive white collar and rump patches.
